h: Bridges, Boats and the Fife Coast
p: North Queensferry is an unusual little village, squeezed onto a peninsula under the bridges, and it's well worth more than a quick visit. The Forth Bridge, the great red cantilever railway bridge opened in 1890, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and from the village shore you can see it alongside the Forth Road Bridge and the newer Queensferry Crossing. Three centuries of engineering in one view.

From South Queensferry on the opposite bank, boat trips run out on the Forth in the warmer months, including sailings to Inchcolm Island with its medieval abbey and resident seals and seabirds. It's a lovely follow-up to an aquarium, seeing some of the same creatures out in the wild.

The Fife Coastal Path passes right through North Queensferry, so walkers can head east towards Inverkeithing and Aberdour, where there's a castle and a popular sandy beach called Silver Sands. Dunfermline, a short drive inland, is the ancient capital of Scotland with its abbey and palace ruins.

Getting there is easy: North Queensferry has its own railway station on the line from Edinburgh, and it's a short downhill walk to the aquarium. Remember the walk back up is steeper. The village has a couple of cafés and a pub for refuelling afterwards. On a clear day, the bridge views alone are worth the trip.
